back: Not merely the absence of disease or physical fitness, but a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being.
Any organism - bacterium, virus, fungus, protozoan or helminth - that causes disease in man.
Caused by Salmonella typhi, which enters the small intestine through contaminated food and water and migrates via blood. Confirmed by the Widal test.
Mary Mallon, a cook who was a typhoid carrier and spread typhoid for several years through the food she prepared.
Caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae; the alveoli fill with fluid, causing severe breathing problems. Spread by droplets and by sharing utensils.
Caused by rhino viruses, which infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs. Symptoms usually last 3 to 7 days.
A toxic substance released when red blood cells rupture in malaria; responsible for the chill and high fever recurring every three to four days.
The female Anopheles mosquito - it is both the vector and one of the two hosts the parasite needs.
Caused by Entamoeba histolytica in the large intestine; houseflies act as mechanical carriers from faeces to food.
Caused by Ascaris, the common round worm; eggs pass out in faeces, contaminate soil, water and plants, and are taken in with contaminated food or water.
Caused by Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi; chronic inflammation of the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs, transmitted by female mosquito vectors.
Fungal infection by Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton; dry scaly lesions on skin, nails and scalp. Heat and moisture make it thrive in skin folds.
The overall ability of the host to fight disease-causing organisms, conferred by the immune system. It is of two types: innate and acquired.
Non-specific defence present at the time of birth, provided by four barriers: physical, physiological, cellular and cytokine.
Proteins secreted by virus-infected cells that protect non-infected cells from further viral infection - the cytokine barrier.
Pathogen-specific immunity characterised by memory: a low-intensity primary response on first encounter, and an intensified secondary (anamnestic) response on later encounters.
Four peptide chains - two light and two heavy - so represented as H2L2. Types include IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG.
The antibody mediated response, carried out by antibodies produced by B-lymphocytes and found in the blood.
The immune response mediated by T-lymphocytes; it allows the body to differentiate self from nonself and is responsible for graft rejection.
Immunity in which the host produces its own antibodies after exposure to antigens - through natural infection or vaccination. It is slow to develop.
Immunity produced by giving ready-made antibodies directly - for example colostrum (IgA) for the infant, antibodies crossing the placenta, and antitoxin for tetanus.
Introducing antigenic proteins of a pathogen, or an inactivated/weakened pathogen, so the body raises antibodies and memory B and T-cells against it.
Direct injection of preformed antibodies - as with antitoxin in tetanus or antibodies against snake venom.
The exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens in the environment (allergens); the antibodies involved are of IgE type.
Chemicals released from mast cells that produce the symptoms of an allergic reaction. Anti-histamine, adrenalin and steroids relieve them.
A condition in which the body attacks its own self-cells, due to genetic and other unknown reasons. Rheumatoid arthritis is an example.
Bone marrow and thymus - where immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes.
Spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches of the small intestine and appendix - sites where lymphocytes meet antigen and become effector cells.
Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, present in the lining of the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts; about 50 per cent of the lymphoid tissue in the human body.
Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome - deficiency of the immune system acquired during the lifetime, so it is not a congenital disease. First reported in 1981.
Human Immuno deficiency Virus, a retrovirus with an envelope enclosing an RNA genome. It uses reverse transcriptase to make viral DNA from its RNA.
Helper T-lymphocytes. HIV infects and destroys them repeatedly, so their number falls progressively and the patient becomes immuno-deficient.
Enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay - the widely used diagnostic test for AIDS.
Drugs used to treat AIDS. They are only partially effective - they prolong life but cannot prevent death.
The property of normal cells by virtue of which contact with other cells inhibits their uncontrolled growth. Cancer cells have lost it.
A mass of proliferating neoplastic cells that grow rapidly, invade and damage surrounding tissues, starve normal cells of nutrients, and metastasise.
The property of malignant tumors in which cells sloughed from the tumor travel through blood and start new tumors at distant sites.
Physical, chemical or biological agents that transform normal cells into cancerous neoplastic cells - for example X-rays and UV, tobacco smoke, and oncogenic viruses.
A piece of suspected tissue is cut into thin sections, stained and examined under a microscope by a pathologist (histopathological study) to detect cancer.
Substances such as alpha-interferon given to cancer patients because tumor cells avoid the immune system; they activate the immune system to destroy the tumor.
Drugs that bind specific opioid receptors in the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. Heroin (diacetylmorphine) is the common example, made by acetylation of morphine.
Chemicals from the inflorescences of Cannabis sativa that interact with cannabinoid receptors mainly in the brain; used to make marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja.
Coca alkaloid from Erythroxylum coca that interferes with the transport of dopamine; a potent central nervous system stimulant causing euphoria, and hallucinations in excess.
Taking drugs for a purpose other than medicinal use, or in amounts or frequency that impair one's physical, physiological or psychological functions.
The alkaloid in tobacco that stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline, raising blood pressure and increasing heart rate.
The period between 12 and 18 years of age - both a period and a process - a bridge linking childhood and adulthood and a vulnerable phase of mental development.
A psychological attachment to certain effects of drugs and alcohol, such as euphoria and a temporary feeling of well-being, that drives repeated use even when it is self-destructive.
The tendency of the body to manifest a characteristic and unpleasant withdrawal syndrome - anxiety, shakiness, nausea and sweating - if the regular dose is abruptly discontinued.
With repeated use of a drug, the tolerance level of the receptors increases, so they respond only to higher doses - leading to greater intake and addiction.

Females: masculinisation, abnormal menstrual cycles, excess facial and body hair, deepened voice. Males: reduced testicle size, decreased sperm production, baldness, prostate enlargement. Adolescents: stunted growth.
